question: A 32-year-old man presents with 5 days of fever, chills, and a new cardiac murmur. Which physical examination finding most strongly supports a diagnosis of infective endocarditis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Splenomegaly can occur in endocarditis but is a non-specific finding shared with many febrile illnesses including malaria and typhoid.

answers.text: Janeway lesions (non-tender haemorrhagic macules on palms and soles)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Janeway lesions are non-tender, non-blanching haemorrhagic macules on the palms and soles; they are septic embolic lesions pathognomonic of infective endocarditis.

answers.text: Generalised lymphadenopathy with posterior cervical chain prominence

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Posterior cervical lymphadenopathy points more towards EBV/infectious mononucleosis than endocarditis.
Rose spots are characteristic of enteric fever (typhoid), not infective endocarditis.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the peripheral signs of infective endocarditis: Janeway lesions (non-tender, palms/soles), Osler nodes (tender, finger pads), splinter haemorrhages (nails), Roth spots (retinal haemorrhages with pale centres).

Well done. Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, splinter haemorrhages, and Roth spots are peripheral stigmata of infective endocarditis — always examine the palms, nails, and fundi in a febrile patient with a murmur.
